title: datasette-apps 0.4a0
summary:
Release: datasette-apps 0.4a0

Datasette Apps are sandboxed HTML and JavaScript applications that live inside Datasette - think Claude Artifacts, but these ones can run SQL queries against your data.

0.4a0 adds support for linking: you can link to an app with #fragments in the URL and the app can see and use those, plus supported URL schemes are reported back to Datasette Agent so it can help write apps that link to each other.

This means you can have e.g. an app that shows details about a specific record, and a completely separate app that searches those records and links to their representations in the first app.

title: Duplicate Vector Search Chunks: Deterministic IDs Beat Random IDs During Ingestion
summary:
A page-change alert fires, and its vector search results contain duplicate chunks from the same paragraph under different IDs. The page did not change three times. The ingestion job did.

TL;DR: A retried or re-run bulk ingestion probably inserted identical chunks under fresh random vector IDs. Derive each vector ID from the document ID and chunk index, so a repeat overwrites the same records instead of appending more. If a new parse can produce a different number of chunks, delete the old records by document ID before upserting the replacement set. Then assert that the indexed count for that document equals the parser's output.

For a web-page watcher, that is the difference between an alert grounded in one current passage and an alert assembled from duplicate evidence. It also changes the first diagnostic question: inspect identity and cardinality before tuning similarity thresholds or adding a reranker.

title: Your iOS App Says “Offline”—But Is It? Debugging API Failures With a VPN Enabled
summary:
A user connects their iPhone to a VPN, opens your app and sees:

No internet connection. Please try again.

They switch to another app, which works.

Your app may have encountered a real failure. But “no internet” might be the wrong diagnosis.

A hostname lookup can fail. A secure connection can fail. An API can return an authentication error. The response can arrive successfully and then fail JSON decoding.

A failed API operation does not automatically mean the device is offline—or that the VPN caused the failure.

The first useful fix is to preserve those distinctions in your networking code.

Start with what actually failed

Think of an API operation as several stages:

  1. Establish a usable network connection.
  2. Resolve the destination hostname when needed.
  3. Establish the secure connection.
  4. Exchange the HTTP request and response.

title: Raw public keys move TLS identity into provisioning and rotation
summary:
Raw public keys move TLS identity into provisioning and rotation

Most TLS deployments rely on X.509 certificates to connect a public key with a name and a chain of trust. RFC 7250 defines another option: sending a raw SubjectPublicKeyInfo value in TLS or DTLS and learning the peer identity from an external mapping. The protocol still authenticates possession of the private key, but it does not perform certificate path validation for a peer certificate.

This design is useful for constrained devices and closed systems where a full certificate profile is unnecessary. It also moves a large amount of security responsibility into provisioning. The verifier must know which raw public key belongs to which peer and must reject keys that are not on that list. A successful handshake with an unknown key is not an identity match.

title: Stop showing a spinner: stream an AI answer's progress in 40 lines of Python
summary:
A question about your data can take ten seconds or more to answer properly. Ten seconds of spinner feels broken. Ten seconds of visible progress feels like work being done.

This post shows how to read a streamed answer with nothing but requests: progress lines first, then the rows, then the answer. It uses server-sent events (SSE), so the same pattern applies to any API that streams this way.

The format in 30 seconds

An SSE response is plain text. Each event is two lines, then a blank line:

event: status
data: {"stage": "generating_sql", "message": "Generating SQL..."}

So the reader is a small loop: remember the last event: line, parse the next data: line as JSON, act on the pair.
